GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Move two triangles and watch how their matching lines and side crossings line up; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag a corner or a whole triangle, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Press Direct or Converse to switch views, and Reset to start over.

Drag A1, B1, C1, A2, B2 or C2, or focus one and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps). You can also drag either shaded triangle as a whole.

Look for the math

Two different-looking drawings turn out to say the same thing. The live cut-the-knot page now embeds a GeoGebra picture; the Java applet this port follows is preserved in the 2006 Wayback capture. Both give the same theorem, and this page keeps the old applet's two views and its six draggable corners.

Two ways to line things up

Write the first triangle as A1 B1 C1 and the second as A2 B2 C2. The page asks about two conditions:

1. The lines A1A2, B1B2, C1C2 are concurrent (they pass through one point).
2. The crossings ab = A1B1 ∩ A2B2, bc = B1C1 ∩ B2C2 and ca = C1A1 ∩ C2A2 are collinear (they lie on one line).

Desargues' theorem says 1 always implies 2. Its dual says 1 follows from 2, so for this theorem the dual is the converse too. The page's condition 1 prints "B2B2" once; that is a typo for B1B2, as its own proof and applet make clear. The applet never forces either condition: you drag freely and it shows whichever construction you chose.

What the two buttons draw

Direct joins matching vertices and puts a yellow dot at the average of the three pairwise line crossings when they are within 8 board units of one another. That is the perspective centre from condition 1. Converse draws the six side lines, marks ab, bc, ca, and joins them with a magenta axis. In 1,500 triangles built to share a centre, the three crossings lined up with a maximum error below 1e-6 units; in 1,500 triangles built to share an axis, the three vertex lines met with the same accuracy. The logic test also checked the page's Menelaus calculation: the product of its three directed ratios is −1 in every such case.

Why a third dimension helps

The page's proof (kindly supplied by Hubert Shutrick) lifts one triangle out of the plane. Two triangles that do not lie in one plane have planes meeting in a line; the side crossings of condition 2 must lie on that line, and the vertex lines of condition 1 meet at the point where the three joining planes meet. Project the picture back down and the flat theorem follows. This is why the result is a projective one, though a flat proof needs more care.

The page excludes a few exceptional positions, for example A1, A2, B1, B2 all on one line. The old applet shows that too: when two lines are parallel their crossing is NaN, so there is no yellow dot and the magenta axis is extended from the crossing that still exists. The test compares its NaN and extension behaviour directly with the bytecode.

Try Converse, then drag C2 until the three side crossings sit on a straight line; switch to Direct and watch the yellow centre appear.
